title: Ποταμὸς καὶ βύρσα
part: The River and the Hide (Chambry 320 · Perry 368)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 320 (= Perry 368). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποταμὸς δι’ αὐτοῦ βύρσαν βοείαν φερομένην ἰδὼν ἠρώτησε· « Τίς καλῇ ; »
sentences.tr: Potamos di’ autou byrsan boeian pheromenēn idōn ērōtēse· « Tis kalēi ; »
sentences.l: A river, seeing an ox-hide being carried through himself, asked: « What are you called? »
sentences.i: A river saw an ox-hide being carried down his stream and asked: « What are you called? »
sentences.n: δι’ αὐτοῦ, 'through himself' — the river is both the place and the speaker. φερομένην is the passive participle: the hide does not travel, it is carried. καλῇ is second person present passive of καλέω, 'you are called'. Chambry sets a space before the Greek question mark; that spacing is his, and it is kept in the Greek line only.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ εἰπούσης· « Σκληρὰ καλοῦμαι, » ἐπικαχλάσας τῷ ῥεύματι εἶπεν· « Ἄλλο τι ζητεῖ καλεῖσθαι· ἐγὼ γὰρ ἤδη ἁπαλήν σε ποιήσω. »
sentences.tr: Tēs de eipousēs· « Sklēra kaloumai, » epikachlasas tōi rheumati eipen· « Allo ti zētei kaleisthai· egō gar ēdē hapalēn se poiēsō. »
sentences.l: And she having said: « I am called Hard, » he, plashing loudly with his stream, said: « Seek to be called something else; for I shall presently make you soft. »
sentences.i: When she answered: « I am called Hard, » the river splashed up loudly in his current and said: « Look for some other name — I shall soon make you soft. »
sentences.n: Τῆς δὲ εἰπούσης is a genitive absolute, the construction that carries most of the background action in these fables. Σκληρά is given as a name, not a description — the hide answers the question as though introducing herself. καχλάζω is the noise of water breaking and splashing, and the compound ἐπι- sets that noise over the hide; the derision is in the act, not in the word, which is not the Greek verb for laughing. ζητεῖ is printed with the accent of a third-person indicative, 'he seeks', where the sense wants the imperative ζήτει, 'seek'; the Greek is left exactly as Chambry prints it and the English follows the sense — the same kind of printed oddity as ποιεῖ at fable 199.

sentences.t: Ὅτι τολμηρὸν ἄνδρα καὶ αὐθάδη πολλάκις εἰς γῆν κατήγαγε συμφορὰ βίου.
sentences.tr: Hoti tolmēron andra kai authadē pollakis eis gēn katēgage symphora biou.
sentences.l: That an over-bold and self-willed man, a mischance of life has often brought down to the ground.
sentences.i: The story shows that a mischance of life has often brought the over-bold and self-willed man down to the ground.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. κατήγαγε is a gnomic aorist — a past tense stating what always happens, which English renders with the present or the present perfect. τολμηρός is daring, and in this company over-bold; αὐθάδης is 'self-pleasing', the man who consults nobody but himself. The object stands first, as in the Greek, so that the subject συμφορὰ βίου arrives last, where the sting is.
